business.what_it_does: Fathom provides a cookieless, privacy-focused website analytics dashboard that shows which pages are popular, who's sending traffic, and which campaigns and events convert, without tracking individual visitors.
business.business_model: subscription, tiered by monthly pageviews across all a customer's sites, with a 7-day free trial and no free tier

facts.statement: Fathom describes itself as 'Analytics without the cookies' and as a Google Analytics alternative that respects visitor privacy.

provenance.quote: Analytics without the cookies ... Fathom is a Google Analytics alternative that makes your analytics easy to understand and respects visitor privacy.

facts.statement: Fathom is used by Microsoft, Tailwind and over a million websites, including Huberman Lab (powered solely by Fathom).

provenance.quote: Trusted by Microsoft, Tailwind & over a million websites ... Analytics for Huberman Lab are solely powered by Fathom.

facts.statement: EU Data Isolation is enabled by default on every plan, including the smallest: EU visitors' personal data is processed in the EU, while anonymized analytics are stored on US infrastructure.

provenance.quote: EU visitors’ personal data stays in the EU. Anonymized analytics are stored on our US infrastructure. ... Is Data Isolation available to me on my current plan? Yes. Every plan includes Data Isolation, including the smallest. It’s enabled by default.

facts.statement: EU isolation also routes traffic from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom as if EU, and Fathom's EU servers are in Falkenstein, Helsinki and Nuremberg.

provenance.quote: It includes visitors from the following non-eu member nations: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, United Kingdom ... Our EU server locations: Falkenstein, Helsinki, Nuremberg

facts.statement: Customers who need all global traffic routed through the EU can switch to an 'Extreme EU Isolation' script endpoint.

provenance.quote: If you need to use Extreme EU Isolation, where all global traffic is routed through the EU, please use https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js instead.

facts.statement: Installation is done by adding Fathom's embed script to a site's header, via the WordPress plugin or one of Fathom's other integrations, and verified by watching the Realtime visit count on the dashboard.

provenance.quote: To start collecting data from your website, you need to install our script in the header of your site’s code via our WordPress plugin or using one of our integrations. Fathom’s dashboard is live and real-time, so the best way to check if our script is installed is by visiting your website and seeing if your visit shows up in the “Realtime” count at the top of your dashboard.

facts.statement: Customers can block local, staging or test environments from Fathom so that non-live pageviews don't count against the plan's pageview quota.

provenance.quote: If you use local, staging, or test environments, you can keep those visits out of Fathom so your analytics only reflect real traffic to your live website. This also prevents non-live pageviews from counting against your plan quota.

facts.statement: Fathom offers a GA4 importer that brings historical Google Analytics 4 data into the Fathom dashboard at no extra charge, and that imported history remains viewable and exportable while the subscription is active.

provenance.quote: Import supported Google Analytics 4 data into your Fathom dashboard, then keep measuring with simple, privacy-focused analytics. We don’t charge extra for historical imports. Your imported history stays available to view and export while your Fathom subscription is active.

facts.statement: Fathom sells software rather than user data, positioning this as the reason its plans are paid rather than free.

provenance.quote: Fathom Analytics sells software, not data. If you aren’t paying for the product, you are the product. That’s why we charge a fair price for our software because we feel it’s a more honest business model.

facts.statement: Fathom does not offer sales calls or live demos; prospects instead watch a walkthrough video, click through a live demo dashboard, or run a 7-day trial alongside their existing analytics.

provenance.quote: We don’t do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our 10-minute walkthrough, click around the live dashboard or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics.

facts.statement: Fathom does not offer a free plan.

provenance.quote: Do you offer a free plan? Nope, and here’s why: we’ve invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure...

facts.statement: Fathom has a dedicated site firewall settings feature for keeping data clean, though the specific mechanics are not captured in this excerpt.

provenance.quote: Site firewall settings - Fathom Analytics ... Support home / Keep your data clean

facts.statement: Fathom explicitly maintains separate marketing pages addressing agencies and European companies as distinct buyer segments, alongside comparison pages against Google Analytics, Matomo, Cloudflare Web Analytics and Jetpack Stats.

provenance.quote: Website analytics for: European companies, Agencies ... Compare Fathom with: Google Analytics, Matomo, Cloudflare Web Analytics, Jetpack Stats

facts.statement: Marketing copy states features load without cookie notices and describes the product as GDPR compliant, while a separate documentation page states GDPR compliance happens by default for every customer on every plan without setup.

provenance.quote: With Fathom Analytics, there's no setup or knowledge required to comply with GDPR; that happens by default for every customer on every plan.

entries.claim: EU isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer, with nothing to set up, tweak, or change in the embed script to use it.
entries.verbatim: If you want to use [EU isolation](https://usefathom.com/features/data-isolation), congratulations; as a Fathom customer, you’re already using it, and it’s enabled by default!

entries.claim: Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.
entries.verbatim: There’s nothing you have to set up or tweak or even change in [your embed script](/docs/script/embed) to use it. Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

entries.claim: Fathom's EU isolation treats visitors from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom as EU visitors even though these are non-EU member nations.
entries.verbatim: It includes visitors from the following non-eu member nations: - Iceland - Liechtenstein - Norway - Switzerland - United Kingdom

entries.claim: Fathom's EU servers are located in Falkenstein, Helsinki, and Nuremberg.
entries.verbatim: - Falkenstein - Helsinki - Nuremberg

context.conditions: located under the 'Our EU server locations' heading

entries.claim: For Extreme EU Isolation, where all global traffic is routed through the EU, customers use the script at https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js instead of the default embed script.
entries.verbatim: If you need to use Extreme EU Isolation, where all global traffic is routed through the EU, please use `https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js` instead.

context.subject: Extreme EU Isolation (Fathom Analytics)
context.conditions: requires loading a different script URL

entries.claim: Firewall settings are adjusted by going to Settings, then Sites, clicking the site, then clicking the Firewall tab.
entries.verbatim: To adjust your firewall settings, go to `Settings`, then `Sites`, click on your site, then click the `Firewall` tab.

entries.claim: Fathom's firewall offers separate list tabs for Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, and Events.
entries.verbatim: Open a list tab (Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, or Events).

entries.claim: When pages, IPs, domains, or countries are blocked in the firewall, those visitors can still access and navigate the site; only their data is excluded from the Fathom dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Note: If you've blocked pages, IPs, domains, or countries, visitors coming from those sources will still be able to access and navigate around your site, but their visits just won't be shown as data in your Fathom dashboard.

entries.claim: Pageviews on blocked pages do not count toward a customer's payment plan pageview allotment.
entries.verbatim: Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics payment plans / page firewall
context.conditions: page must be blocked via the firewall's Pages list

entries.claim: Fathom's firewall currently supports wildcards only for IPv4 addresses.
entries.verbatim: **Note:** Currently only IPv4 addresses are supported for wildcards

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall IP wildcards
context.limitations: does not support IPv6 wildcards

entries.claim: Once one or more domains are added to the firewall's allow list, data coming from any other domain is blocked instantly.
entries.verbatim: **Once you add one or more allowed domains, this means data coming from any other domain will be blocked instantly**. This is useful if you do not want to collect data from your local development environment or are worried that other people may be using your script (by accident or otherwise).

context.subject: Fathom Analytics domain firewall
context.conditions: applies once at least one domain is added to the Allow list

entries.claim: A domain wildcard such as *.example.com allows only subdomains like subdomain.example.com and www.example.com, and does not allow the root domain example.com itself.
entries.verbatim: This then allows only subdomains of example.com, so: `subdomain.example.com` and `www.example.com`, etc. But note: using `*.example.com` would not allow `example.com`, so be careful.

entries.claim: The firewall's Events tab can drop junk or unwanted event names at collection time, or allow collection of only the event names sent on purpose.
entries.verbatim: Use the `Events` tab to drop junk or unwanted event names at collect time, or to collect only the names you send on purpose.

entries.claim: In the Events firewall, Block mode drops only the listed event names while still collecting every other event, Allow mode collects only the listed names and wildcard patterns, and an empty Allow list collects every event.
entries.verbatim: **Block** drops those names and still collects every other event. **Allow** collects only the names (and wildcard patterns) on the list. An empty allow list collects every event.

entries.claim: After saving a change to the IP firewall list, the new list takes effect starting with the next visit.
entries.verbatim: The next visit after you save uses the new list.

entries.claim: After saving a change to the Events firewall list, the new list takes effect starting with the next event.
entries.verbatim: The next event after you save uses the new list.

entries.claim: The firewall only stops future visits from being recorded; removing spam already present in reports requires using the separate Data removals feature in a site's Manage settings.
entries.verbatim: The firewall stops future visits. To clean up spam that’s already in your reports, use `Data removals` in your site’s `Manage` settings.

entries.claim: Fathom's tracking script can be installed via Fathom's WordPress plugin or via one of Fathom's other integrations.
entries.verbatim: To start collecting data from your website, you need to [install our script](/docs/script/embed) in the header of your site’s code via our [WordPress plugin](/docs/integrations/wordpress) or using [one of our integrations](/docs/integrations)).

entries.claim: Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time, so script installation can be verified by visiting the site and checking whether the visit appears in the Realtime count at the top of the dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Fathom’s dashboard is live and real-time, so the best way to check if our script is installed is by visiting your website and seeing if your visit shows up in the “Realtime” count at the top of your dashboard.

entries.claim: Once allowed domains are set, Fathom filters out data from any hostname that is not on that list, including local, staging, and test domains.
entries.verbatim: Once allowed domains are set, Fathom filters out data from any hostname that is not on that list, including local, staging, and test domains.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics site firewall (allowed domains)
context.conditions: Requires configuring allowed domains in site firewall settings.

entries.verbatim: This also prevents non-live pageviews from counting against your plan quota.

entries.claim: Filtering by IP address works well for a single developer or a small, stable set of IP addresses, but allowed domains are more reliable for teams and changing networks.
entries.verbatim: This works well for a single developer or a small, stable set of IP addresses, but allowed domains are more reliable for teams and changing networks.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics IP exclusion vs allowed domains
context.conditions: Comparing IP-based exclusion to domain-based exclusion for blocking non-live traffic.

entries.claim: A visitor can block Fathom tracking for themselves by running fathom.blockTrackingForMe(); in the browser console on a page where Fathom is installed, which stores the setting in the browser's local storage so it keeps working for future visits from that browser.
entries.verbatim: fathom.blockTrackingForMe();

context.subject: Fathom Analytics browser console blocking
context.conditions: Must be run in the browser console on a page where Fathom is installed; stored via local storage.

entries.claim: Fathom shows analytics in real time, so a non-live visit that is correctly excluded will not show up as a current visitor.
entries.verbatim: Fathom shows analytics in real time, so if the exclusion is working, your non-live visit should not show up as a current visitor.

entries.verbatim: Since Fathom is a Canadian corporation (eh), we’ve implemented strict Data Isolation, allowing you to comply with GDPR while ensuring EU visitor IP addresses never reach US-servers.

entries.claim: If a company is based outside the EU, Fathom automatically routes its EU visitors to EU servers.
entries.verbatim: **If you’re a company outside the EU**, then you still will no doubt have visitors from the EU. Fathom takes care of routing all your EU visitors to EU-servers for you, automatically.

context.subject: Fathom customers based outside the EU

entries.claim: For visitors outside the EU, Fathom's EU-owned CDN (Bunny.net) sends their pageview directly to Fathom's US servers and anonymizes their IP address data there.
entries.verbatim: **If a visitor is outside the EU**, our EU-owned CDN (Bunny.net) sends their pageview to our US servers directly and anonymizes their "data" (IP address).

entries.claim: Fathom uses Bunny.net, described as an EU-owned CDN, to route visitor traffic for Data Isolation.
entries.verbatim: **If a visitor is outside the EU**, our EU-owned CDN (Bunny.net) sends their pageview to our US servers directly and anonymizes their "data" (IP address).

entries.claim: For visitors inside the EU, Fathom's CDN sends their pageview to European servers, strips the IP address inside the EU before it reaches US infrastructure, and stores only anonymous data on its US servers.
entries.verbatim: **If a visitor is inside the EU**, our CDN sends their pageview to our European servers and anonymizes their data immediately. The IP address (personal data under GDPR) is stripped from the request inside of the EU and never reaches our US infrastructure. The anonymous data is then stored on our main US servers for fast and easy retrieval on our customer dashboards, but there’s zero personal data associated with any of it.

entries.claim: Fathom's EU Cloud is monitored 24/7, highly available, and multi-region, with enough capacity to process very high ('Bieber-level') traffic.
entries.verbatim: Our EU Cloud is monitored 24/7, highly available, multi-region and has enough capacity to process Bieber-level traffic.

entries.claim: Fathom doesn't use cookies, so no cookie consent banner is needed on the site.
entries.verbatim: You don’t need a consent banner that annoys visitors, clutters your layout and slows the page down. Fathom [doesn’t use cookies](/why-fathom-analytics/cookieless-analytics), so you can keep analytics on your site without the pop-up.

entries.claim: Fathom is GDPR, ePrivacy, PECR and CCPA compliant.
entries.verbatim: We’re GDPR, ePrivacy, PECR and CCPA compliant because digital privacy sits at the core of the product.

entries.claim: Privacy lawyers have vetted how Fathom collects and stores data, and EU visitor data is processed in the EU automatically.
entries.verbatim: We’ve had privacy lawyers vet how we collect and store data, and EU visitor data is processed in the EU automatically.

entries.claim: Fathom filters out bots, crawlers, DDoS junk and other non-human traffic so the dashboard reflects real visitors.
entries.verbatim: We filter out bots, crawlers, DDoS junk and other non-human traffic, so your dashboard is a picture of people who actually visited.

entries.claim: Fathom data shows up in real time, not 24 to 48 hours later.
entries.verbatim: Data shows up in real time, not 24 to 48 hours later.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics
context.limitations: No named comparator for the '24 to 48 hours' contrast.

entries.claim: Users can combine filters into a named saved view (e.g. blog traffic, a campaign, or a country) that everyone with site access can reopen in one click.
entries.verbatim: Want to check your blog traffic, a campaign or visitors from a particular country? Combine filters, give the view a name and open it again in one click. Everyone with access to that site can use the same saved views.

entries.claim: Users can mark a launch, redesign or press mention on the traffic chart as a milestone.
entries.verbatim: Mark a launch, a redesign or a press mention on your chart with a milestone.

entries.claim: Users can compare traffic across the previous week, month, year, or custom periods.
entries.verbatim: Compare dates to see how traffic changed from the previous week, month or year, or choose your own periods.

entries.claim: Fathom can record newsletter signups, form submissions and purchases as events.
entries.verbatim: Record newsletter signups, form submissions and purchases as events.

entries.claim: Fathom lets you send a value with a purchase event and choose the event's currency, so sales totals show alongside completion counts.
entries.verbatim: Send a value with a purchase and choose the currency for your events, so you can see sales totals alongside completion counts.

entries.claim: Fathom uses UTM tags to distinguish newsletters, ads and social campaigns, and the dashboard can be filtered by campaign to see its traffic, pages visited and events completed.
entries.verbatim: Use UTM tags to tell your newsletters, ads and social campaigns apart. Filter the dashboard by a campaign to see its traffic, the pages people visited and the events they completed.

entries.claim: Fathom can schedule weekly or monthly report emails to the account holder, colleagues or clients, combining multiple sites in one email with each recipient getting selected sites.
entries.verbatim: Schedule weekly or monthly emails for yourself, colleagues or clients. Send a report for one website, or bring several sites together in the same email. Each recipient gets the sites you select.

entries.claim: Every Fathom plan includes at least 50 sites, with extra site packs available.
entries.verbatim: Every plan includes at least 50 sites, with extra packs available.

entries.claim: Fathom offers an all-sites view to check multiple sites together before opening one for details.
entries.verbatim: Check them together in the all-sites view, then open a site for the details.

entries.verbatim: Share individual dashboards publicly or protect them with a password.

entries.verbatim: Download CSV files for a spreadsheet or report, or use our API to bring Fathom data into your own tools.

entries.verbatim: Download CSV files for a spreadsheet or report, or use our API to bring Fathom data into your own tools.

entries.verbatim: Import historical GA4 data, and connect Google Search Console to see search terms, clicks, impressions and search positions alongside your website analytics.

entries.verbatim: Import historical GA4 data, and connect Google Search Console to see search terms, clicks, impressions and search positions alongside your website analytics.

entries.claim: Fathom can be installed by adding one line of JavaScript, or via an existing integration, without touching templates.
entries.verbatim: Add one line of JavaScript, or use one of our integrations if you’d rather not touch templates.

entries.claim: Fathom's tracking script loads asynchronously so it doesn't block page loading, and measures traffic without a bulky analytics script.
entries.verbatim: Our small script loads asynchronously, so it doesn’t hold up the rest of your page. You can measure your traffic without adding a bulky analytics script.

entries.claim: Every Fathom plan includes ongoing data retention, letting customers revisit old campaigns and compare year over year since installation.
entries.verbatim: Every plan includes ongoing data retention. Come back to an old campaign, compare this year with last year, or see how far your site has come since you first installed Fathom.

entries.claim: Fathom is built to handle traffic spikes and large, high-traffic websites.
entries.verbatim: A launch or a popular post can bring a lot of visitors at once. Fathom is built to handle traffic spikes and large websites, so you can keep an eye on what’s happening.

entries.claim: Fathom does not use cookies, which is why no consent banner is needed for analytics.
entries.verbatim: No. That’s why you don’t need a consent banner for analytics. You can read more about how we process data on our [data journey page](/data).

entries.claim: Fathom Analytics is GDPR compliant.
entries.verbatim: Yes. Privacy law comes before features we could otherwise build. You can read more about [our GDPR-compliant website analytics](/legal/compliance/gdpr-compliant-website-analytics).

entries.claim: Fathom's anonymisation methods are documented, and EU visitor data is handled with data isolation.
entries.verbatim: We’re open about how data is processed and stored. Our anonymisation methods are documented, and EU visitor data is handled with [data isolation](/features/data-isolation).

entries.claim: Fathom is a hosted-only product that processes pageviews on a global CDN, keeps EU visitor data processed in the EU, and routes everyone else to the closest region.
entries.verbatim: No. Fathom is a hosted product so we can process pageviews on a global CDN, keep dashboards fast, and process EU visitor data in the EU. Everyone else is routed to the closest region.

voice.tone: Confident and plain-spoken, with a quiet dig at competitors' privacy practices; avoids hype words and lets facts do the selling.
voice.rhythm: Short declarative sentences mixed with one longer explanatory sentence per paragraph; paragraphs are compact, often two to three sentences.
voice.person: Writes as "we"; the product itself sometimes gets agency ("Fathom shows you...").
exemplars: Switching analytics doesn’t have to mean starting from zero. Import supported Google Analytics 4 data into your Fathom dashboard, then keep measuring with simple, privacy-focused analytics.
We don’t charge extra for historical imports. Your imported history stays available to view and export while your Fathom subscription is active.
Lots of analytics software claims to comply with various privacy laws, such as GDPR, PECR or the ePrivacy Directive, but most of them are putting you and your website visitors at risk.

Fathom shows you what's working on your website without tracking the people who visit it. It's trusted by Fortune 100s, banks, governments and companies of every size. Start with a 7-day free trial, then plans start at $15/month.

segments.name: A bootstrapped SaaS founder who is also the only developer, opening GA4 once a week and closing it again without an answer
segments.situation: He runs one or two paid products plus a marketing site, a docs site and a changelog, all deployed from the same laptop. He writes the launch post, ships the feature and answers the support email in the same afternoon. Analytics is a tab he opens when something feels off or something good happens — a launch, a mention in a newsletter, an unexplained signup spike — and GA4 makes him choose a property, fix a date range and then hunt through reports to find out which post sent the people who started trials. He also has local and staging environments hitting the same tracking script, so the numbers he does look at are quietly wrong. He optimised his page weight on purpose and then put a tag manager and a consent banner on top of it because someone told him he had to. objections.objection: Google Analytics is free and I am currently paying nothing for this. $15 a month to look at visitor counts on a site that barely has any is a subscription I will cancel in three months.
objections.answer: There is no price answer — Fathom confirms there is no free plan and argues the paid model is the point: it sells software, not data, and prices for sustainability (E204, E205, E233), with the explicit claim that Google Analytics is free because Google monetises the visitor data customers hand over (E255 — Fathom's own assertion about a rival, not independent verification). What is concretely on the table at the bottom tier: $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews with 50 sites included (E148, E159, E163), the same analytics features as every other plan (E194), 2 months free on yearly billing (E161), and cancel-anytime with no contracts (E199). For the multi-site freelancer the 50 included sites make the per-site cost the real argument; for a single low-traffic site the evidence offers no discount, only a values argument.

provenance.quote: Nope, and here’s why: we’ve invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure (we don’t host Fathom on cheap servers that go offline). Our business model is selling software, not your data, so we’ve priced Fathom to be sustainable for a very long time.

objections.objection: A single-page dashboard cannot do what I actually use analytics for — funnels, cohorts, where people drop out of signup, which touch gets the credit. 'Simple' means 'missing the reports my decisions depend on'.
objections.answer: Partly unanswerable, and the gap is deliberate: Fathom does not track individuals (E137), so user-level journeys, cohorts and multi-touch attribution are not coming. What the evidence does support is a named, finite surface — live visitors, total visitors, pageviews, top pages, referrers, countries, devices, browsers, events and UTM campaigns (E73) on one page (E72, E58) — plus combinable saved views any teammate can reopen (E113), date comparison against previous week/month/year (E115), milestones on the chart (E114), events for signups, form submissions and purchases with a value and currency so sales totals sit next to completion counts (E116, E117, E166), campaign filtering that shows a campaign's traffic, the pages visited and the events completed (E118), Search Console terms, clicks, impressions and positions alongside analytics (E126, E142), and CSV export plus an API on every plan for anything else (E123, E124, E170). Nothing in the evidence offers funnel visualisation, cohort retention or session replay; a performance marketer who needs those should be told plainly they are not here.

objections.objection: Moving means abandoning years of history. I will not be able to compare this quarter to last year, and my old data is the only reason I keep the Google property alive.
objections.answer: Mostly answered, with real limits that must be stated rather than glossed. The GA4 importer authorises the Google account with a button, picks the sites and runs (E70, E49), costs nothing extra (E46), and the imported history stays viewable and exportable while the subscription is active (E47, E141); from then on retention is open-ended while you remain a customer, back to signup (E65, E224, E248, E129). The limits: it brings in supported daily analytics from Google's API, does not recreate every GA4 report and does not import GA events (E50); imported data filters differently and totals can differ between the two tools (E51); Universal Analytics data was deleted by Google in July 2024 and cannot be recovered (E52, E68). And data is queued for deletion on cancellation, so exports must happen before leaving (E66, E199).

objections.objection: Our legal and procurement people will not accept a vendor's own web page saying 'GDPR compliant'. They will ask for a DPA, an audit report, a sub-processor list and a data flow diagram — and I am not fighting that battle to save a few pounds.
objections.answer: Strong on substance, thin on third-party attestation. Substance: EU isolation is on by default for every customer on every plan with nothing to configure (E1, E28, E43, E63); EU visitors' personal data is processed in the EU and only anonymised analytics are stored on US infrastructure (E27, E41), with the IP address stripped inside the EU so it never reaches US infrastructure (E41, E36, E37); non-EU visitors route directly to US servers and are anonymised there (E39); the EU servers are named — Falkenstein, Helsinki, Nuremberg (E4) — the CDN is EU-owned Bunny.net (E40), UK, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein traffic is treated as EU (E3), and customers who need all global traffic in the EU can switch to the Extreme EU Isolation endpoint (E5). Fathom says privacy lawyers vetted how it collects and stores data (E110), that Data Isolation was built with EU legal experts, that as a Canadian corporation it is covered by Canada's EU adequacy decision (E213, E36), that it never uses cookies (E82), anonymises IPs, URL parameters and precise location by default (E80, E81, E83), never tracks keystrokes (E84), can honour DNT (E139), and is GDPR, CCPA, ePrivacy and PECR compliant (E109, E214, E95). Gap to disclose: every compliance claim here is a vendor statement or its own documentation — the evidence contains no SOC 2 or ISO certificate, no named DPA, no sub-processor list and no independent audit, so a procurement reviewer who wants a document rather than a claim cannot be satisfied from what we know.

objections.objection: Our policy says analytics data stays on infrastructure we control, so I need to self-host. Or: I will not put the one dataset I cannot rebuild inside a vendor I cannot run myself.
objections.answer: Not answerable — and the evidence says so outright: Fathom is hosted-only, by design, so it can process pageviews on a global CDN, keep dashboards fast and process EU visitor data in the EU (E134). This buyer is disqualified rather than persuaded; the evidence itself points at the open-source on-premise alternative with unlimited retention (E59, E64). The nearest partial consolations are CSV export and the API (E123, E124, E170), export of everything back to day one (E225), and all-traffic-through-the-EU routing (E5) — none of which is self-hosting. Copy should not argue this one.

provenance.quote: No. Fathom is a hosted product so we can process pageviews on a global CDN, keep dashboards fast, and process EU visitor data in the EU. Everyone else is routed to the closest region.

objections.objection: A card up front for a 7-day trial, and they will not even get on a call with me. I do not hand card details to a tool I have not seen working on my own site, and seven days is not long enough to decide.
objections.answer: Half answered. Fathom states plainly that it does no sales calls or live demos, and offers instead a 10-minute dashboard walkthrough video, a clickable live demo dashboard that needs no signup, and a trial run alongside existing analytics (E203, E74, cta-live-demo). On the card: it is required, but it is not charged until the trial ends and Fathom emails before billing starts (E160, E198); cancellation is self-service in account settings with no contracts and no call required (E199). Verification is fast — one line of JavaScript or an integration (E127, E226, E25), or the WordPress plugin with no template editing (E96, E18), then watch your own visit appear in the Realtime count (E19, E228). What nothing in the evidence offers: a longer trial, a free tier, or a human on a call for a buyer who wants one before paying.

provenance.quote: We don’t do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our [10-minute walkthrough](/video/dashboard-walkthrough), click around the [live dashboard](https://app.usefathom.com/demo) or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics.

objections.objection: Metered pageviews mean the one month I actually get traffic is the month I get punished — surprise overage, or worse, the dashboard switched off exactly when I need it.
objections.answer: Well answered. Fathom says it never charges for occasional traffic spikes and does not shut the account off on hitting the limit (E251); if usage stays well over, it emails about a larger plan and the customer chooses (E252, E200); there are several friendly reminders and extra time before dashboard and API access is paused, and data keeps being collected throughout (E253, E200). Tier changes require two consecutive months over or under, and downgrades are self-service from billing settings (E202). Quota can also be protected: blocked pages do not count as pageviews against the allotment (E9), and blocking local, staging and test environments keeps non-live pageviews off the quota (E20, E21). Honest counterweight — custom events, whether from the site or the API, each count towards the monthly pageview allowance (E201, E196), and the allowance is shared across all sites (E196, E232), which matters most to the agency buyer.

provenance.quote: If you exceed your limit for two months in a row, we’ll get in touch about a larger plan. Or, if you’re under your current tier for two months in a row (and it’s not our lowest tier already), you can move to a smaller plan from your billing settings.

objections.objection: Any JavaScript analytics undercounts — a third of my audience blocks trackers. I would be paying for numbers that are just as wrong as the free ones, only now from a vendor with no second source to check against.
objections.answer: Not answered by the evidence. Fathom says it filters bots, crawlers, DDoS junk and other non-human traffic so the dashboard reflects people who actually visited (E111) and that it is built to show human visits (E215), and one customer calls the data accurate (E211) — but nothing in the ledger states how Fathom behaves against blocklists or quantifies recovery versus Google Analytics, so the undercounting worry cannot be beaten with what we currently know. The only honest move in copy is the side-by-side trial: run Fathom next to existing analytics and compare the two yourself (E198, E227, E203). Do not claim blocker immunity.

objections.objection: I already moved off Google Analytics to a privacy-friendly tool. Migrating twice in two years, re-installing scripts and losing continuity again is not happening for a slightly nicer dashboard.
objections.answer: Largely unanswered for the specific rivals this buyer has. The evidence only supports comparisons against Google Analytics, Matomo, Cloudflare Web Analytics and Jetpack Stats — nothing addresses the other cookieless tools a reader may already run. Against Matomo specifically: GDPR compliance requires no setup or knowledge and happens by default on every plan, where the rival's GDPR manager and IP anonymisation require setup and knowledge to use correctly (E63, E61, E79); the script is a few KB, deferred and CDN-served versus 20KB (50KB with more features) needing your own CDN (E75, E77); retention is open-ended while subscribed versus up to 24 months on the rival's cloud product (E65, E64); and the GA import is a few button clicks versus generating a Google Cloud API key (E70, E69). Against Cloudflare, the evidence establishes only that it exists, is free and launched end of 2020 (E91) — no differentiator is proven. Switching-cost relief that applies to anyone: one line of JavaScript or an existing integration (E127, E226, E231), GA4 history importable free (E46, E70), and running in parallel during the trial (E227).

objections.objection: This is a script that counts pageviews. I could log them myself, or stick the free Cloudflare one on and be done — paying monthly forever for something I could knock together is irritating on principle.
objections.answer: Weakly answered, and worth being honest about. The evidence does not argue against building your own at all; it argues that free rivals are funded by visitor data (E136, E255 — Fathom's own unnamed-competitor assertion) and that Fathom invested in fast, reliable infrastructure rather than cheap servers (E206, a vague unmeasured claim). What is genuinely tedious to build and is included on every plan: EU-isolated routing by default with servers in three EU cities (E1, E4, E28), bot and crawler filtering (E111, E169), real-time reporting (E112, E228), open-ended retention back to day one with export (E65, E225), 50 sites on one account with an all-sites view (E163, E219, E121), scheduled multi-site email reports to clients or colleagues who never log in (E119, E223), shared or password-protected dashboards (E122), firewall controls for spam, staging and junk events (E6, E7, E11, E13), traffic-spike capacity (E130, E42), and an API (E170, E124). The maintenance argument, not the counting argument, is the only one the evidence supports.

provenance.quote: Other analytics products can afford to be “free” because they profit from what they collect about your visitors.

objections.objection: My clients asked for Google Analytics by name, and the report they get has to look like it came from my studio, not from a tool they have never heard of. Re-educating twelve clients costs me more than the reporting does.
objections.answer: Partly answered, with a real gap. On the table: every plan includes at least 50 sites with up to 15 packs of 50 more at $10/month or $100/year, self-service from billing (E120, E163, E197, E162, E93); weekly or monthly scheduled report emails to the client directly, combining several sites in one email with each recipient getting only the sites you choose (E119, E223); dashboards shared publicly or password-protected so a client never needs a login (E122); an all-sites view for checking everything at once (E121, E219); a dashboard described as understandable without months of training (E58, E72); and GA4 history imported so the client's old numbers still appear (E46, E70, E141). The gap: nothing in the evidence establishes white-labelling, custom branding, agency sub-accounts or per-client user permissions, so a studio that must present reports as its own cannot be promised that from what we know.

objections.objection: Switching analytics is never at the top of the list. It works well enough, nobody is asking me to fix it, and I will look at it next quarter.
objections.answer: Barely answerable — nothing in the evidence creates a deadline, and the one dated forcing event has already passed: Google deleted Universal Analytics data in July 2024, and no importer can recover what Google no longer holds (E52, E68), which argues for acting before more history ages out rather than for acting today. The only levers are low friction and reversibility: one line of code or an existing integration (E127, E226, E231), install verified in minutes via the Realtime count (E19, E228), run in parallel with no disruption to current reporting (E227, E198), cancel anytime with no contract (E199), and free GA4 import whenever it happens (E46). Treat timing as the objection most likely to kill a send, and do not pretend urgency the evidence does not support.

**Shared category vocabulary.** Two or more competitors use these. Keep the words needed to explain the product; common vocabulary alone does not make a proposition generic. Avoid unsupported superlatives:

map.reading:
Assessment summary. Verified quotations do not establish demand or purchase intent; commercial priority remains a hypothesis.
- A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report: review first; product compatibility supported; audience evidence supported (7 quoted source(s)); use or purchase captured; reachability venue identified.
- The person at a European company who has been told, by someone with authority, that Google Analytics has to go: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (3 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A clinic group or telehealth startup rebuilding its public marketing site after the tracking-pixel settlements: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A small nonprofit or advocacy site whose visitors would be endangered by ad-tech trackers: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (2 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A freelancer or small studio who installs analytics on every client site and gets asked for the numbers by people who will never log in: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence absent (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A US business that just received a CIPA 'wiretapping' demand letter naming the scripts on its website: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability unknown.
- A small EU-selling ecommerce brand whose consent banner is eating a third of its own sales data: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (3 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability unknown.
map.note: Coverage gaps and failures: (1) Direct buyer-voice forum threads were hard to surface — three attempts at Reddit and Hacker News practitioner threads on freelance multi-client analytics and Ghost/newsletter publishers returned vendor comparison pages instead, so the freelancer segment leans on the existence of a reporting-tool market rather than quoted complaints. (2) No churn evidence found: searches for people who left or cancelled Fathom turned up only review-site remarks that it is 'expensive for what you get' and costs more per pageview than Plausible past 1M views, with no first-person account — real churn reasons remain unknown. (3) Security posture unverified: a search for Fathom Analytics SOC 2/BAA returned results for an unrelated AI meeting-notes company also called Fathom, so treat any certification claim as unconfirmed and do not reuse those hits. (4) No named EU public-sector or university procurement decision was found, so the institutional variant of the compliance buyer is unsupported and was not proposed as a separate segment. (5) Search scope was left empty, so no geography was imposed; German-language vocabulary was tried once and returned agency listicles rather than buyer discussion. (6) Population counts are unknown throughout, fit is left at zero, and assessment fields are left at defaults for separate validation. (7) The Shopify candidate has no documented install path in the supplied capability catalogue — verify before using it. (8) One source (clickport) is a vendor-adjacent guide and one (levelup) is a practitioner essay; both should be read as advocacy, and the consent-loss percentages they cite differ widely and need independent checking.

counterevidence_summary: Technically literate site owners in this crowd default to free hosted or self-hosted analytics when volume is low and the site is non-commercial. — A no-cost substitute that satisfies the same 'is anyone reading this' need directly competes with a paid subscription that has no free plan. Review before prioritising.

The no-consent-banner argument is openly contested in this audience on ePrivacy grounds, so it cannot be assumed to close the sale. — For this segment the dominant stated driver is GA's complexity and distrust, not banner removal, so a disputed banner claim is an argument to avoid rather than a blocker. Minor condition; does not exclude this audience.
reasons: OpenCage — a small, founder-run geocoding API business whose engineer writes the stack posts — publicly documents stopping Google Analytics and paying for Fathom, which is both usage and a stated paid relationship from a member of this exact segment.

Data Isolation on every plan with no setup, which is the answer to her mis-configuration liability (fact_a0b032ff6b62bdc4); EU-company traffic processed inside EU borders with IPs never reaching US infrastructure (fact_fba50d7e9ff1a526); automatic routing of EU visitors for non-EU-based customers (fact_f9f45e566ff968b6); IP stripped inside the EU before US storage (fact_9762f46e7f54c895); the honest scope limit she must forward — personal data in the EU, anonymised analytics on US infrastructure (fact_86ff0fccbb67ea7e); named EU server locations (fact_6386e33b15bd62c8); European-owned routing infrastructure, the fact that also carries the Canadian adequacy point (fact_2f5e055893599edf); and no consent notice required for GDPR, the measurement loss she is trying to recover (fact_ae1db331d1fd624d). reasons: A named EU store is documented running GA4 alongside a consentless tool and finding GA4 short by a large share of visits, which substantiates the data-loss pain this candidate is built on.

Product truth supports events with monetary value (fact_6d62dda6fa0a130f, fact_486fbb13f13c8965), UTM campaigns (fact_1617e70865c6f135, fact_c8eecfc1f1492aad), bot filtering (fact_4b55b21278852d23) and no banner requirement (fact_8a3614eb808af0b7).

Product fit rechecked: Her job is attributing orders to newsletters and ads without depending on consent clicks. Purchase events carrying a value and currency, so sales totals sit beside completion counts (fact_5f8cf11bfb733f3d); UTM campaign filtering down to pages visited and events completed, which is the newsletter/ad decision (fact_2ec7532745790fb4); no consent banner required for the analytics, the premise of the whole purchase (fact_fb419c1c90b8607c); automatic bot filtering so the numbers reconcile against orders (fact_f9ed624f45a4b72e); and a single line of code that works with every site, web app and CMS as the only available install route (fact_c6d3d3217cf599bc). Two plan conditions are required because they govern her tier: pageviews and custom events share one allowance (fact_c7c3cc34a81d6799) and each custom event counts against the monthly pageview allowance (fact_8ece01f3527059e5) — an event-heavy store moves tiers. Still unsupported: the integration list (fact_b95c1ce13e57dbae) names no Shopify or WooCommerce app, so the native-app-only disqualifier stands, and the catalogue contains no checkout funnel, product-level or multi-touch attribution capability — automatic channel decomposition is not answered by referrer and UTM reporting.
unknowns: Compatibility is unresolved: no Shopify or WooCommerce install path appears in the supplied integration list, and no fetched source establishes whether a header-script install is acceptable to this buyer or whether a native app is required.
No EU store in the corpus is observed buying Fathom; the named example belongs to a competing vendor's case study.
How events sharing the pageview allowance (fact_5e4b5202d97bd55f) affects a store's tier is untested in any source.
No public venue reaching these store owners was fetched — the Shopify community threads referenced in the hypothesis are not in this corpus.
Review the counterevidence before prioritising this audience.

ranked_relevance.why: Documents the mechanism that answers the defining need: all data on one page, filterable without training, versus multi-step report configuration.
Documents the live real-time dashboard, which matches the researched workflow of frequent launches needing an immediate read and no researched problem id is required for it.
Documents self-install as a single line of code across any site, web app or CMS, and that it can run alongside the incumbent script, which fits a founder who owns the tag himself.
States the mechanism (no cookies) and its direct consequence (no consent banner) for the banner problem.
Most specific documented performance mechanism for the page-weight problem: a few KB, deferred load, CDN delivery.
States what the single dashboard actually shows (pages, sources, campaigns, events), which is the concrete content behind the simplicity claim.
Documents the exact install step (one header line with the Site ID) behind the self-install mechanism.
Documents the Site ID that the snippet, integrations and API all require, a documented condition of install.
Absolute statement of the cookieless mechanism that underpins the no-banner consequence.
Ties the no-consent-notice claim to GDPR and to the page-load saving from dropping a consent manager.
Documentation statement of asynchronous loading, the behaviour behind the no-slowdown claim.
Documents bot and crawler filtering, which explains why counts differ from the incumbent and supports the simple-numbers need.
Documents the GA import path for a buyer who already has an analytics script live.
States the documented exception to the importer mechanism (no full GA4 report recreation, no GA events), required alongside E74.
Names Next.js, Nuxt, Ghost and Webflow, which match the researched optional stack signal for this self-deploying founder.
Documents allowed-domain filtering of local, staging and test hostnames, relevant to a founder who deploys his own site.
Documents the console command to block the owner's own visits, a concrete mechanism for a one-person site.

problem_fits.caveat: The catalogue documents a single-page, filterable, real-time dashboard; it does not document funnels, cohorts or session paths, so 'simpler' means fewer capabilities, not the same capabilities arranged better.
problem_fits.why: Documented mechanism (one dashboard page showing pages, sources, campaigns and events, live) directly matches the complaint of multi-step report configuration; the supporting testimonials are opinions, so this is not SOLVED.

problem_fits.caveat: The no-banner statement is a vendor claim scoped to Fathom's own analytics; any other cookie-setting script on the founder's site is outside it, and the researched complaint comes from 2021 and 2023 sources whose present applicability is not corroborated.
problem_fits.why: The cookieless mechanism and the stated consequence (no consent notice required for the analytics) answer the banner complaint directly.

problem_fits.caveat: Concrete caveat: the selected evidence gives only 'a few KB', 'deferred' and 'asynchronous' with no measured PageSpeed figure and no stated comparison to Google Analytics, so the buyer's own 96-to-81 datapoint cannot be matched with a licensed number; the KB comparison in the audience source is the buyer's, not ours.
problem_fits.why: Real product mechanisms exist for script weight and blocking behaviour, but the magnitude of improvement is not established by the selected evidence.

dossier.audience_name: A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report
dossier.orientation: Fathom Analytics is hosted, cookieless website analytics that a founder installs himself with one script line and reads on a single real-time dashboard instead of configuring GA4 reports.

ranked_relevance.why: Documents the mechanism that answers the defining need: all data on one page, filterable without training, versus multi-step report configuration.
Documents the live real-time dashboard, which matches the researched workflow of frequent launches needing an immediate read and no researched problem id is required for it.
Documents self-install as a single line of code across any site, web app or CMS, and that it can run alongside the incumbent script, which fits a founder who owns the tag himself.
States the mechanism (no cookies) and its direct consequence (no consent banner) for the banner problem.
Most specific documented performance mechanism for the page-weight problem: a few KB, deferred load, CDN delivery.
States what the single dashboard actually shows (pages, sources, campaigns, events), which is the concrete content behind the simplicity claim.
Documents the exact install step (one header line with the Site ID) behind the self-install mechanism.
Documents the Site ID that the snippet, integrations and API all require, a documented condition of install.
Absolute statement of the cookieless mechanism that underpins the no-banner consequence.
Ties the no-consent-notice claim to GDPR and to the page-load saving from dropping a consent manager.
Documentation statement of asynchronous loading, the behaviour behind the no-slowdown claim.
Documents bot and crawler filtering, which explains why counts differ from the incumbent and supports the simple-numbers need.
Documents the GA import path for a buyer who already has an analytics script live.
States the documented exception to the importer mechanism (no full GA4 report recreation, no GA events), required alongside E74.
Names Next.js, Nuxt, Ghost and Webflow, which match the researched optional stack signal for this self-deploying founder.
Documents allowed-domain filtering of local, staging and test hostnames, relevant to a founder who deploys his own site.
Documents the console command to block the owner's own visits, a concrete mechanism for a one-person site.
Licenses the GDPR compliance statement that sits behind the banner answer.
Closest buyer analogue in the ledger, a solo software founder, speaking to the simple interface; opinion only, not a measured outcome.
Founder-level statement on simplicity and accuracy; attributed opinion, not a measurement.
Customer statement pairing privacy with not bogging down load times, the two researched complaints; qualitative only.
Developer-credible customer logos (GitHub, Laravel, Bootstrap, HashiCorp) for a technical buyer; logo placement only, no usage detail.
Verbatim duplicate of E97; using both would double-count one opinion.
Verbatim duplicate of E197 from a second page; redundant.
Unverifiable 'only choice' superlative aimed at governments and finance; wrong scale and wrong register for a solo founder.
Vendor characterisation of Google rather than a product fact; the ledger flags the superlative as unverified.
Weak, unnamed enterprise proof (Fortune 100s, banks, governments) that does not speak to a one-person site.
True and licensed, but 50-site plans and extra packs are not the researched need of a founder running one self-built site.
An SEO expert's opinion about privacy and simplicity; background only, and an opinion is not a description of what the dashboard does.
WordPress framing; the audience evidence does not establish WordPress as this buyer's stack.

problem_fits.caveat: The catalogue documents a single-page, filterable, real-time dashboard; it does not document funnels, cohorts or session paths, so 'simpler' means fewer capabilities, not the same capabilities arranged better.
problem_fits.why: Documented mechanism (one dashboard page showing pages, sources, campaigns and events, live) directly matches the complaint of multi-step report configuration; the supporting testimonials are opinions, so this is not SOLVED.

problem_fits.caveat: The no-banner statement is a vendor claim scoped to Fathom's own analytics; any other cookie-setting script on the founder's site is outside it, and the researched complaint comes from 2021 and 2023 sources whose present applicability is not corroborated.
problem_fits.why: The cookieless mechanism and the stated consequence (no consent notice required for the analytics) answer the banner complaint directly.

problem_fits.caveat: Concrete caveat: the selected evidence gives only 'a few KB', 'deferred' and 'asynchronous' with no measured PageSpeed figure and no stated comparison to Google Analytics, so the buyer's own 96-to-81 datapoint cannot be matched with a licensed number; the KB comparison in the audience source is the buyer's, not ours.
problem_fits.why: Real product mechanisms exist for script weight and blocking behaviour, but the magnitude of improvement is not established by the selected evidence.

segment_objections.objection: I already have GA4 running; switching means abandoning the history I have.
segment_objections.answer: Fathom's GA4 importer needs only an account authorisation, a site selection and a run, but it brings in supported daily analytics from Google's API rather than recreating every GA4 report or importing GA events, and it cannot recover Universal Analytics data because Google deleted it in July 2024.

segment_objections.objection: The numbers will not match what Google Analytics reports, so I will not trust them.
segment_objections.answer: The script can run alongside the current analytics during evaluation, and the documented reasons for divergence are stated: Fathom filters bots, crawlers and other non-human traffic, and imported GA4 data has different filtering options with totals that can differ between the two tools.

segment_objections.objection: I want to own and host the analytics data on my own server rather than hand it to another third party.
Google Analytics is free; why pay for this on a side project?
Installing another script will cost me the page speed I just got back.
segment_objections.answer: The embed code is a few KB, loads deferred and asynchronously so it does not hold up the page, and dropping a cookie consent manager removes that load as well; no measured PageSpeed figure is established by the selected evidence.
